name: Deep Orient Blue
lede: Deep Orient Blue is a greyed, dusty blue from Ridgway's 1912 chart, its name a reference to the East Asian porcelain and textile blues the nineteenth century called "oriental," not a measured match to any one craft.

sections.title: A trade word, not a recipe
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 plate XXXIV gives this hue the name Deep Orient Blue, hue 45′′, tone i, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the nearest category as "grayish blue" in its block 186 [1]. "Orient" and "oriental" were common nineteenth-century trade words for blues associated with East Asian porcelain, lacquer and dyed cloth; Ridgway's chart carries a small family of them, including the lighter [[dark-orient-blue]] and the brighter [[dusky-orient-blue]] [1]. None of our sources ties this particular swatch to a named porcelain or dye [2].

In LCH terms it measures lightness 52, chroma 15, hue 249 degrees, Munsell 0.4PB 5.1/3.8 [1]. Its closest match in the library is [[delft-blue]], about 3.2 CIEDE2000 units away, with [[light-tyrian-blue]] close behind at 3.9 units [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A match within six CIEDE2000 units covering at least five percent of the canvas turns up in 237 of our 23,781 archive paintings, about one percent, as photographed [4]. It peaks in the 1920s, in 6 of 237 paintings, at 3.4 times the overall rate, and is most loved by Claude Monet, in seven of his fifty paintings here, fourteen times his own museums' baseline; it most often plays a mid-tone, in 55 percent of its appearances [4].

The earliest dated match is Michele Giambono's *Saint Peter*, 1445, more than four and a half centuries before Ridgway recorded the name in 1912; early centuries are thin in the archive, so this is a floor, not a first, and a photograph of an aged canvas is a screen color, not a pigment test [4].
